selectedPapers.title: Dynamic responses of floating offshore wind turbines under freak waves: A review
Dynamic reliability framework for resilience assessment for floating offshore wind turbines
selectedPapers.abstract: Floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) are becoming an important part of future energy systems and can complement conventional energy grids in supporting overall energy safety and security. Understanding the dynamic reliability evolution of FOWTs under hazardous events and degradation-induced failures remains largely unexplored and represents a major scientific challenge. Existing monitoring systems, such as SCADA, have limited capability to identify the true root causes of component-level failures. Consequently, maintenance actions may target incorrect or incomplete failure sources, while undetected root causes may continue to propagate residual damage and accelerate degradation of other components. This study develops a dynamic reliability assessment framework for resilience-oriented recovery management of FOWTs under hazardous conditions. A Bayesian Network is employed to represent the hierarchical FOWT system and model the propagation of component-level failures to subsystem- and system-level functionality degradation. During recovery, the framework captures the effects of residual damage from unidentified or incompletely repaired root failures on subsequent reliability evolution. A condition-aware deep inspection module is introduced to represent a PHM-enabled recovery process. Although this strategy requires additional inspection effort and decision-making resources before maintenance, it can more accurately identify root causes and propagation pathways, supporting more effective recovery decisions. A case study demonstrates that system reliability can decrease rapidly when critical components are affected by hazardous events. It further shows that experience-based recovery can partially restore system functionality but may fail to eliminate residual damage when root causes are not fully identified. In contrast, the condition-aware strategy achieves greater reliability restoration by improving root-cause identification and repair effectiveness. The results reveal the importance of integrating condition-aware inspection into post-disaster recovery planning and highlight the value of dynamic reliability assessment for resilience improvement in FOWTs. Specifically, the study quantifies the reliability benefits gained from condition-aware inspection during post-disaster recovery.

selectedPapers.title: Combined optimisation of anchors and mooring systems for floating offshore wind turbines over rock seabeds
selectedPapers.abstract: As commercial interest in floating offshore wind turbine (FOWT) projects increases, research into mooring system design for these devices has become prevalent in academia. While some research into FOWT mooring system optimisation has been published, this work does not account for the cost of the anchors, which must be sized according to the mooring system loads and form a substantial part of the FOWT system cost. This thesis seeks to reconcile anchor and mooring design for FOWT projects through the development of an optimisation tool for minimising the total cost of both the anchors and mooring system. The Anchor Optimisation Design Tool (AODT), created for and detailed in this work, uses numerical modelling and a genetic algorithm method to determine the optimal geometry and cost for a groutless rock anchor in a given design load and set of geotechnical conditions. These groutless rock anchors used the Swift Anchor design by SCHOTTEL Marine Technologies (SMT), and were optimised to find the lowest total manufacturing and installation cost. In developing the installation cost model for the AODT, a new numerical model for predicting Swift Anchor drilling times was derived, validated and presented in this thesis. The Mooring Optimisation Design Tool (MODT) was developed to find the mooring design parameters with the lowest total anchor and mooring system cost for a given FOWT platform and environment. The MODT also used a genetic algorithm optimisation method, and evaluated potential mooring configurations using a combination of dynamic simulations in OrcaFlex and interpolation using the kriging method. The MODT accessed data generated by the AODT to predict the anchor cost of each mooring system under evaluation, based on the anchor loads observed. The MODT was used to optimise a nylon rope mooring system for a 15 MW FOWT on a semi-submersible platform in 8 case studies. The principles of the AODT were applied to create an equivalent anchor cost model representing traditional drilled and grouted piles. Mooring optimisations were run for both anchor types, so to observe the affects of anchor type on the optimal system design and cost. The case studies show using Swift Anchors over traditional drilled and grouted rock anchor technology allows a 45.0% to 55.5% cost reduction of the total anchor and mooring system, depending on environmental factors. The method of combined anchor and mooring system optimisation detailed in this thesis presents a significant step forward in optimisation of balance of plant systems for FOWT, and has potential for finding substantial cost savings in future FOWT projects.

selectedPapers.title: Wind speed estimation using second-order sliding-mode observers: simulation and experimental validation on a floating offshore wind turbine
selectedPapers.abstract: Abstract. Rotor-effective wind speed (REWS) estimation is crucial for the control and performance optimization of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs). This paper introduces a robust estimation framework based on second-order sliding-mode observers (SOSMOs), developed in both constant-gain and adaptive versions. The observers are developed using a reduced-order dynamic model and validated in the OpenFAST simulation environment when all degrees of freedom are activated. Their performances are compared with the continuous–discrete extended Kalman filter (CD–EKF) used in the reference open-source controller (ROSCO). The proposed approach is assessed under stochastic wind/wave conditions through OpenFAST simulations and further validated experimentally using a scaled software-in-the-loop (SIL) setup. Simulation results indicate that the proposed observers perform comparably to the CD–EKF in terms of estimation accuracy while offering robustness, simpler implementation, and reduced computational complexity.

selectedPapers.title: Physics-informed probabilistic neural network for reliable condition assessment and failure prognosis of substructures in floating offshore wind turbines
Large-eddy simulation of the IEA 15 MW wind turbine using a two-way coupled fluid–structure interaction model
selectedPapers.abstract: Abstract. The aim of this work is to study the aeroelastic response of the IEA 15 MW Reference Wind Turbine (RWT)using a high-fidelity fluid–structure interaction solver that combines large-eddy simulation with a modal computational structural dynamics solver through a two-way coupling. The fluid solver employs the actuator line model to simulate the interaction between the turbine blades and the fluid and the immersed-boundary method to model the presence of the tower and nacelle. The results are compared with those obtained by the OpenFAST software, which is a well-known numerical tool for engineering predictions. A series of simulations have been performed with and without the presence of the tower and nacelle to better understand the effects of these components on flow structures and structural deformations. The largest discrepancies among the solvers have been observed in correspondence with the blade passage in front of the tower, which induces an abrupt alteration in the local incidence angle of the flow. Moreover, by comparing the outcomes of different structural approximations, it has been established that taking into account the torsional degree of freedom affects the deformations, aerodynamic loads, and power coefficient considerably. On the other hand, the non-linearity of the solver appears to have a weak effect on the same quantities.
